newsitem.title: UK: Soyinka calls for sanctions on Nigeria.
newsitem.headline: Soyinka calls for sanctions on Nigeria.

text.p: Exiled Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka called on Thursday for an oil embargo and immediate sanctions against the military regime in Nigeria.
Soyinka, a leading opponent of Nigerian military leader Sani Abacha, is being tried in absentia on treason charges. He said measures stronger than words or gestures were necessary.
"There is no merit in talking directly to Sani Abacha. He is totally impervious to dialogue," the poet, playwright and novelist told a news conference.

"Increased sanctions. Isolation, cultural, economic, diplomatic, cutting off sporting links, an embargo on further mineral exploration -- in other words an oil embargo against Nigeria, would be of a far-reaching effect," he added.
Soyinka denied an oil embargo would hurt ordinary Nigerians because the oil boom had no impact on ordinary people.
"Oil money has gone into the pockets of a small coterie," he said. "There is no reason why profiteers should not experience the privations ordinary people have suffered."
Soyinka, the first African to win the Nobel prize for literature, was forced into exile in 1994 after Abacha annulled elections designed to return the country to democratic rule.
He was one of 12 dissidents charged with treason in March following a spate of bombings in Nigeria.
Nigerian police blamed the umbrella opposition group NADECO (National Democratic Coalition) and its foreign affiliates for the bombings.
Soyinka refused to condemn the bombings. He said they were only directed at the military who were oppressing the population.
He stood by his description of Abacha as a murderous imbecile and the military regime as a gang of torturers and assassins.
"I wonder how I won a prize for literature," he said. "I keep running out of expressions to describe them."

The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) met in London on Thursday to hear Nigerian opposition leaders and human rights activists to help them to decide whether to recommend tougher action against the regime at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Edinburgh in October.
Nigeria was suspended by the 53-nation group in 1995 after the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight minority rights activists.
Soyinka said CMAG had no option but to recommend the immediate implementation of sanctions.
He was in Edinburgh to receive an honorary doctorate from the university.
